content:
The first Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) estate built using the "Modular Integrated Construction" (MiC) method, On Pak Court in Kwun Tong, has been occupied for only 15 months. Recently, owners have reported that the exterior wall paint is peeling, blistering, flaking off, and even growing moss. When "The Collective" visited the site on Thursday (the 8th), they observed suspended platform workers painting in multiple locations, and the exterior walls no longer showed blistering. However, the adjacent MiC-built On Wah Court also has large-scale blistering on its exterior walls, a situation similar to On Pak Court. The estate perimeter wall also shows numerous cracks, with efflorescence seeping out. Some residents fear that problems will persist after the Housing Department's maintenance period expires, at which point owners will have to pool funds for repairs, complaining that they "spent millions on a defective building," and hoping the Housing Department will maintain the estate's common areas permanently.

On Pak Court and the adjacent On Wah Court are the first HOS estates to adopt the MiC construction method by the Housing Department. Residential units are prefabricated in mainland factories, with the structure, plumbing and electrical systems, and interior finishes all completed before being transported to Hong Kong and assembled into buildings.

Blistering on On Wah Court Exterior Walls

When "The Collective" visited Anderson Road this afternoon, they observed that repair work on the exterior walls of On Pak Court had largely been completed, while the estate perimeter wall still showed signs of water seepage and cracks. However, On Wah Court, also built using MiC and located just one street away, has similar problems with its exterior walls. One entire facade of the 28-storey building shows blistering across the full wall surface, with the joints between floors showing obvious unevenness. The estate perimeter wall has numerous fine diagonal cracks in multiple places, with efflorescence seeping out and leaving white crystalline deposits on the surface. On Wah Court residents Mr. and Mrs. Cheung said they had only moved in two months ago, with no leaks inside their unit, but they noticed paint peeling and flaking from the orange sections of the exterior wall.

Recently, some On Pak Court owners have approached the media, reporting that the residents' group chat contains numerous complaints about continuous leaks since the building was occupied. Some had water seepage in their kitchens and toilets when they took possession of their units, while the building walls also showed large-scale blistering and paint flaking, with water seeping from exterior pipes and growing moss. Others reported cracks in the exterior walls of upper floors, and the sealing strips between modular units shrinking and cracking.

Toilet Pipe Leakage Discovered

Ms. Wong, an On Pak Court resident, took possession of her unit about six months ago. She told "The Collective" that she discovered a leaking toilet pipe at the time, which was repaired by the contractor, and there have been no seepage problems inside the unit since. However, she is dissatisfied that a new building has already had paint flaking after just one year of occupation, and is worried about further problems after the maintenance period expires: "What if we owners have to pool money for major repairs?" Ms. Wong hopes the Housing Department will "honor its quality guarantee" and permanently handle maintenance of common areas. She added that suspended platform workers have been carrying out repairs at the estate recently, and paint has splattered onto her laundry, forcing her to dry clothes indoors. She stated bluntly: "I spent millions buying a defective building."

Cracks Appeared in Canopy Shortly After

Another owner, Ms. Tsang, moved in at the beginning of this year. Cracks appeared in the canopy shortly after, which were repaired by the contractor. She does not know whether "in wind and rain" such cracks will reappear in the future. She noted that fortunately, the owners have been united enough to contact the District Council and the media for follow-up, which has compelled the Housing Department to carry out repairs. She is not currently worried about having to bear high maintenance costs in the future.

On Wah Court was built by Shui On Construction and completed in August last year, with occupation beginning in November. On Wah Court's two towers provide 990 units, ranging from 296 to 495 square feet, at an average price of HK$7,030 per square foot, with units selling for HK$1.81 million to HK$3.77 million. On Pak Court was a concurrent project by the same contractor. Foundation work began in February 2022, with completion three years later. The single tower contains 420 units with usable areas ranging from 291 to 498 square feet, at an average of HK$7,000 per square foot, selling for HK$1.77 million to HK$3.73 million, with occupation beginning progressively in July last year.

The Housing Department previously replied to the media that after receiving complaints about On Pak Court in late July this year, it immediately urged the contractor to carry out comprehensive repairs. Following drone inspections, it was estimated that local areas of the exterior walls had not been thoroughly cleaned of dust before painting, or the primer had not been applied uniformly, constituting workmanship deficiencies in the painting process.

Furthermore, the department did not find any cracks in the wall structure, believing these were merely water stains on the exterior wall after rain. Regarding allegations that "MiC module sealing strips had shrunk and cracked," the Housing Department confirmed after on-site verification and review of records that this did not match owners' descriptions, but was instead a workmanship flaw where wall paint had overflowed onto the sealing strips during application. Cleaning and repairs at those locations have been completed, and there is no seepage situation in any unit.
